```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("theme.R")
library(housepi)
set.seed(42)
```

Let's briefly recall the concept of Bayesian data augmentation for the case of epidemiological outbreaks.

Bayesian data augmentation is a computational strategy that expands the parameter space by introducing augmented variables (also referred to as hidden or latent variables) to facilitate sampling from the posterior.

Consider a single infectious individual $i$.
Imagine that someone reported the exact time of symptom onset ${t}^{(\mathrm{ons})}_{i}$ .
We can introduce latent infection times ${t}_{i}$, defined as the difference between the onset time and the augmented incubation period ${\tau}^{(\mathrm{inc})}_{i}$:

$${t}_{i} = {t}^{(\mathrm{ons})}_{i} - {\tau}^{(\mathrm{inc})}_{i},$$
where the incubation period is drawn from a model distribution.
Say $x$ the observed data, onset days and status, $h$ the augmented variables infection time and incubation period. If $\theta$ is the vector of parameters, the joint posterior reads

$${P}({\theta}, {h}\vert{x}) \varpropto {P}({x}\vert{\theta},{h}) {P}({h}\vert{\theta}){P}({\theta}).$$
We here explain how to associate individual augmented variables in housepi for minimal examples.

# Build augmented variables

Similarly to parameter, augmented variables require definitions for models and proposals needed for the Bayesian Monte Carlo.
In many applications, augmented variable definitions can also depend on the dataset or on model parameters to be inferred.

## Link arguments to their source

We can declare the source of argument value with the convention `<argument> \@ <source_symbol>`.
E. g. "visit_day\@D" will source the value at individual data "visit_day".

<div style="display: flex; justify-content: center;">
<div>

| Source     | Symbol | Examples          |
|------------|:------:|:-----------------:|
| Augmented  | A      | time OR time\@A   |
| Data       | D      | visit_day\@D      |
| Group Rate | G      | susceptibility\@G |
| Numeric    | N      | 14                |
| Parameter  | P      | mean\@P           |

</div>
</div>

Notice that a variable name without explicit source will automatically be assumed to be an augmented variable.
Similarly, there's no need to explicitate the source of a numeric value. 

More in general, definition arguments `value`, `min`, `max` and `from` can be linked to external values in the following ways

# Status specific definitions

In many applications, the same augmented variable has to be augmented according to different rules according to the individual. 
This is the case for example of infection times for symptomatic and asymptomatic members.
We can address this issue in housepi using status specific definitions, as opposed to generic definitions valid for all positive status individuals.
Let's consider the case of a follow-up that reported symptoms within a follow-up period and tested every household member only at the end.
We use `status = 1` to identify symptomatic individuals and `status = 2` for asymptomatic. 
We augmented infection time of symptomatic as shown in [Get Started](hosuepi.html), i. e. informed by reported onset date.
For asymptomatic members we draw the infection time uniformly within the period of the follow-up.

```{r}
#| warning: false
library(ggplot2)

onset_tommy <- 5
hhmodel <- new_housepi_model("augmented_infection_time") |>
  add_data_wide(data.frame(id = c("tommy", "gina"),
                           status = c(1, 2),
                           onset_date = c(onset_tommy, NA),
                           house_id = "house_1")) |> 
  load_parameter_list(alpha = 0.001, beta = 0.07, gamma = 0.9,
                      size_ref = 4, study_period = 10) |> 

  # associate augmented definitions
  load_augmented_list(
    # augmented infection time for symptomatic members 
    # here we use a generic definition
    infec_time = onset_time - incub_period,
    onset_time = onset_date@D,
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1),

    # augmented infection time for asymptomatic members
    # here we use a status specific definition, with priority over generic
    infec_time = list(status = 2, model = "uniform", 
                      min = !!onset_tommy, max = !!onset_tommy + 10)
  )
```

```{r}
#| fig.alt: >
#|  Density plots of augmented infection times for two household members.
# run inference following traces of specific individuals
hhmodel |> 
  run_inference(steps = 500, id_draws = c("tommy", "gina")) |> 
  get_augm_draws() |> 
  posterior::subset_draws(variable = "infec_time$", regex = TRUE) |> 
  bayesplot::mcmc_dens(facet_args = c(ncol = 1)) +
  geom_vline(data = data.frame(xintercept = onset_tommy),
             aes(xintercept = xintercept), linetype = 2) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = onset_tommy + c(-10, 10))
```

We see that since we assumed the infection of the asymptomatic member to happen after the onset of the index, the model logically makes it more probable to occur closer to that limit.

# Example: estimate incubation periods distribution

For simplicity, we start testing data augmentation on a dataset which is not a household survey.
Instead we consider a simulated report documenting the days when a number of cases were exposed to infection and the days of symptom onset.

```{r}
# use an example script for generate delays
source("generate_delays.R")
# generate delays according to a gamma distribution
dataset <- generate_delays_report(223, mean = 2.2, var = 2.5,
                                  report_error = 0.73)
head(dataset)
```
Note that here the data has no demographic structure: we are implicitly assuming that all individuals live in distinct households.

Assuming the incubation period to be described by a gamma distribution, we want to estimate its parameters augmenting the infection and onset times.
We model both augmented variables as uniformly distributed in the reported ranges.

The model "augmented_example" has the only requirement to associate an augmented `"proba"` to be used as likelihood for each individual with positive status.
This variable will be set to compute the individual log-likelihood according to the incubation period distribution.
We propose the incubation period to be distributed as a gamma distribution, with parameters `shape` and `scale` to be inferred.
Then, we define the augmented variables `infec_time` and `onset_time` as uniformly distributed in the ranges of exposure and onset times, respectively.

```{r}
# generate an instance of the household model class
hhmodel <- new_housepi_model("augmented_example") |>

  # augmented variable definitions as function calls
  load_augmented_list(
    # explicit declaration of incubation period likelihood
    proba = list(
      func = "gamma_meanvar",         # gamma distribution by mean/variance
      func_args = c(x = incub_period, # compute from individual 'incub_period'
                    mean = mean@P,    # use model parameter 'mean'
                    var = var@P),     # and 'var'
      max = 14 # truncate to given maximum
    ),
    
    # declare 'incub_period' as the difference
    # between augmented onset and infection times
    incub_period = .onset_time - .infec_time,
    
    # here we correct right censoring of maximum values
    # to allow for the event to occur during the whole day
    # add 'infec_time' time definition
    .infec_time = list(
      value = exposure_min@D,      # start from data value 'exposure_min'
      model = "uniform",           # uniform within [0, exposure_max + 0.99]
      max = exposure_max@D + 0.99, # min = 0 by default for uniform
      proposal = "normal",         # MCMC proposal is a normal distribution
      proposal_scale = 0.5         # with std. deviation 0.5
    ),
    
    # add 'onset_time' time definition
    .onset_time = list(
      value = onset_max@D + 0.99, model = "uniform",
      min = onset_min@D, max = onset_max@D + 0.99,
      proposal = "normal", proposal_scale = 0.5
    )
  ) |>

  # define the gamma distribution parameter to be inferred
  load_parameter_list(
    mean = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0.1, max = 5, proposal = "normal"),
    var = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0.1, max = 5, proposal = "normal")
  )
```

# Extract augmented variable draws

We could run the inference and extract the results as usual.
However, sometimes we might be interested in extracting also  to check if augmented variables evolve as expected.
We can do so by providing the `id` of individuals whose augmented variables we want to store through the argument `id_draws` of `run_inference()`.

```{r}
#| fig.height: 3
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.alt: >
#|  Trace plots for mean and variance parameters with three parallel chains.
#|  Overlaying orange lines indicate the values used for the simulation.
results <- hhmodel |>
  add_data_wide(dataset) |>
  run_inference(steps = 1000, thin = 10, chains = 3, adapt = 500,
                # store augmented draws of "7" and "13"
                id_draws = c("7", "13"), 
                progress = FALSE)

# plot traces of parameter draws
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_param_draws(results)) +
  geom_hline(data = data.frame(parameter = c("mean", "var"), 
                               simulated = c(2.2, 2.5)),
             aes(yintercept = simulated))
```

```{r}
#| fig.alt: >
#|  Trace plots for individual augmented variables across three MCMC chains.
#|  Incubation period and associated probability for two subjects (IDs 7 and 13).
# plot traces of augmented draws
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_augm_draws(results))
```

In this example we had to introduce auxiliary augmented variables `.onset_time` and `.infec_time`.
The prefix `.` we added to the names is a convention to ensure that housepi will not store the associated draws.

# More about models and proposals

```{r}
#| include: false
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "orange")
```

When it comes to data augmentation, we might need to explore different options for the Monte Carlo moves.
In the following examples we show the differences between move choices that can be performed.
As shown in [Bayesian MCMC options](bayesian_mcmc_options.html), we do the testing with the "blank" model.
We always recommend a visual assessment before choosing a new move.

```{r}
#| warning: false

# with model (default sample)
results <- new_housepi_model("blank") |>
  add_augmented("sample_model", model = "normal", mean = 14) |>
  run_inference()
```

```{r}
#| fig.height: 2
#| fig.alt: >
#|  Trace plot of a single augmented variable sampled from the model.
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_augm_draws(results))
```

```{r}
#| fig.height: 2
#| fig.alt: >
#|  Trace plot of the corresponding model contribution to the log-likelihood.
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_total_log_lik_draws(results))
```

```{r}
#| warning: false
# random walk (without model)
results <- new_housepi_model("blank") |>
  add_augmented("random_walk", value = 14, proposal = "normal") |>
  run_inference()
```

```{r}
#| fig.height: 2
#| fig.alt: >
#|  Trace plot of a single augmented variable without model, i. e. random walk.
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_augm_draws(results))
```

```{r}
#| fig.height: 2
#| fig.alt: >
#|  The flat trace plot of the corresponding log-likelihood shows no contribution.
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(get_total_log_lik_draws(results))
```
